q: What is the purpose of solution evaluation?
options: To write the requirements
To assess whether a solution has achieved the desired business results
To identify the stakeholders
To estimate the project budget and the cost of each remaining product release
explanation: Solution evaluation activities assess whether or not a solution has achieved the desired business results, by comparing actual results with expected values and, over the long term, checking whether the expected business value was achieved.
ref: PMI Guide to Business Analysis, Key Concepts for Solution Evaluation

links.label: PMI Guide to Business Analysis, Key Concepts for Solution Evaluation

q: Which of these is one of the four solution evaluation processes?
options: Determine Viable Options and Provide Recommendation
Conduct Elicitation
Verify Requirements
Obtain Solution Acceptance for Release
explanation: The four processes are Evaluate Solution Performance, Determine Solution Evaluation Approach, Evaluate Acceptance Results and Address Defects, and Obtain Solution Acceptance for Release.
ref: PMI Guide to Business Analysis, Table 1-2

links.label: PMI Guide to Business Analysis, Table 1-2

q: Why should the solution evaluation approach be defined as early as possible?
options: Because the sponsor signs it before the charter
Because it replaces acceptance criteria
Because some metrics need data the product would not otherwise capture, which is costly or impossible to add later
Because evaluation happens before requirements are written
explanation: Some metrics require capturing information beyond what the product itself needs. Without early definition there is a risk that the necessary information will be expensive or impossible to obtain.

q: What is a metric, in solution evaluation?
options: A set of quantifiable measures used to evaluate a solution or business
A type of stakeholder
A stage of the product life cycle, between growth and maturity of the product
A kind of prototype
explanation: A metric is a set of quantifiable measures used to evaluate a solution or business. In solution evaluation it defines how solution performance can be quantified.

q: A proposed metric would be too expensive to collect. What should the team do?
options: Skip evaluation altogether
Collect it regardless of cost
Wait until after the release before deciding what to do
Consider a less costly, next-best alternative
explanation: The cost of capturing and reporting measurements is an important factor. When proposed metrics appear too costly or time-consuming, less costly, next-best alternatives may be considered.

q: In acceptance testing, how is the work divided between testers and business analysis?
options: The business analyst runs all the tests
Testers determine pass or fail; business analysis evaluates the severity, cause and impact of defects and recommends what to do
Testers decide whether to release the product
There is no difference between the two roles
explanation: The pass/fail comparison of results with criteria is typically a testing task. Business analysis then considers the magnitude and severity of the defects, their root cause and risks, and recommends ways to address them.

q: What do "evaluated acceptance results" contain?
options: A comparison of acceptance criteria with actual results, the root cause of variances, the cost to address defects and the business impact
Only a list of passed tests
The project's final budget
The stakeholder register
explanation: Evaluated acceptance results give a summarized comparison between the acceptance criteria and the actual acceptance results, with the root cause for variances or defects, the cost to address them, and the business impact of addressing or accepting them.

q: Two defects are found. One affects a feature tied to the project's top business objective. Which tool shows this link?
options: Stakeholder onion diagram
Persona
Traceability matrix
Product box
explanation: A traceability matrix can be used to assess the business impact of not addressing defects: there could be a significant impact from defects in features that trace to a high-priority objective.

q: Which is NOT one of the recommendations the guide lists for addressing a defect?
options: A workaround in how the product is used
A modification to the product, possibly through a change request
Communication to users about how the product is meant to be used
Deleting the acceptance criterion so the test passes
explanation: Recommendations may include workarounds, modifications to the product, adjustments to how results are measured, investigation of technical causes, and communication to users. Removing a criterion to hide a failure is not among them.

q: On an adaptive project, a story is demonstrated and does not meet its acceptance criteria. What happens?
options: It is accepted anyway to protect velocity
The story can be rejected and returned to the backlog to be reprioritized
The iteration is extended by as many days as it takes for the story to pass
The project is cancelled
explanation: If the demonstration does not prove conformance to the acceptance criteria, the entire story can be rejected and returned to the backlog to be reprioritized. Defects are added to the backlog.

q: Which set lists the bases for a release decision?
options: Acceptable results, organizational readiness, completed transition activities, and acceptance of remaining risks
Budget spent, team size, sponsor's mood, and schedule
The number of requirements written, the number of tests run, the number of defects found, and the number of users
Scope, time, cost and quality
explanation: Release decisions are typically based on the acceptability of the solution, confirmation that the organization is ready, confirmation that transition activities are complete, and acceptance of any remaining product risks and workarounds.

q: Acceptance testing is finished and the analyst has summarized the results. A tester says the test team should now decide whether to release. Who makes the release decision?
options: The business analyst alone, because the analyst wrote the acceptance criteria
The test team
The stakeholders accountable for the product, with the analyst facilitating
The newest team member
explanation: Obtaining solution acceptance gives the stakeholders accountable for the product the opportunity to decide whether it should be released in whole, in part or not at all. The process is one of facilitating that decision.

q: What are the possible release decisions?
options: Approve only
Release fully or partly, delay, or disapprove
Verify or validate
Avoid, transfer, mitigate, accept or escalate
explanation: A release decision may permit the release or partial release of the solution, delay it, or disapprove and prevent it. It often includes a sign-off.

q: A supplier's contract says the new product comes with a 60-day warranty period. What is a warranty period?
options: The time allowed for writing and approving requirements before development is permitted to start
The time before the charter is approved
The length of an iteration
A period after release during which the development team is responsible for fixing defects
explanation: A warranty period is an interval of time during which the product development team is responsible for addressing any defects found after the solution is released for production.

q: What technique is recommended for making a release decision, and why?
options: A facilitated workshop, so all stakeholders hear the reasons for the decision
A survey, so nobody has to meet
Observation, so users are not disturbed
A product box game, so that the team can design the packaging before the release
explanation: Whenever possible, release decisions should be made in a facilitated workshop so that all stakeholders hear the rationale. Summaries of results, remaining risks and unfinished transition activities help decision makers.

q: At the end of an iteration on an adaptive project, the team shows the stories it has finished. How is acceptance of them usually obtained?
options: A formal sign-off by the PMO
A written contract amendment
The product owner's approval at the demonstration that the work meets the definition of done
It is not obtained
explanation: In adaptive approaches, often verbal approval alone is obtained from the product owner, as part of demonstration and feedback, that the solution segment meets the definition of done and can be released.

q: A new ordering system went live three months ago. The analyst now measures whether it is delivering the business value that was expected. When does this evaluation of solution performance usually take place?
options: Before the business case has been written
During elicitation
Before any testing
After the solution has been released
explanation: Evaluation of solution performance typically occurs after a solution has been released, so it is more likely to occur during portfolio or program activities than project activities.

q: Sales were 1,000 units a month before the new system and 1,300 after. How is the business value quantified?
options: As the difference between the baseline and the performance after release: 300 units a month
As 1,300 units a month
As 1,000 units a month
It cannot be quantified
explanation: Performance data before a release are the baseline. If value is measured as increased sales volume, the quantified business value is the difference in sales volume before and after release.

q: The objective of a new intranet is "better informed employees", which cannot be measured directly. What can the team use to evaluate it?
options: Nothing; evaluation is skipped
A proxy, such as task duration, response time or error counts
The sponsor's personal opinion of how well the product is doing
The original estimate
explanation: When performance data cannot be measured for the stated objectives, proxies may be used, such as the average duration of a task, response time or counts of errors.

q: A released product is not delivering the expected value. Interviews reveal nothing. Which technique may uncover that users have invented workarounds?
options: Document analysis
Benchmarking
Observation
Weighted ranking
explanation: Direct observation of users doing their work may uncover workarounds they use to compensate for product gaps. These can be missed in interviews, because long-standing users may not think to mention them.

q: What is the output of Evaluate Solution Performance, and what is it used for?
options: An assessment of business value, used for decisions to enhance, maintain, replace or discontinue the product
A stakeholder register, used for planning communication
A situation statement, used to start elicitation
A charter, used to authorize the project
explanation: The assessment of business value compares expected with actual value and the reasons for the difference. It is used to decide whether to develop a new product or to enhance, retire or discontinue an existing one.

q: Evaluation shows that the remaining planned features would add very little value for their cost. What may the organization do?
options: Build them anyway because they were planned
Double the team
Rewrite the business case so that the result is hidden
End early and move the funds to higher-value work
explanation: Evaluation may identify a point of diminishing returns. Solution evaluation gives teams the ability to end early, even if more functionality could be built, so funds can go to higher-priority work.
ref: PMI Guide to Business Analysis, Key Concepts for Solution Evaluation

links.label: PMI Guide to Business Analysis, Key Concepts for Solution Evaluation

q: Acceptance tests have passed, but the support team is untrained and the cutover checklist is half finished. What should the analyst advise at the release meeting?
options: Release now, because all of the acceptance tests have passed
Delay, because the transition activities are not complete
Cancel the project, because it is clearly not ready
Release now, and train the support team in the weeks afterwards
explanation: A release decision rests on acceptable results, organizational readiness, completed transition activities and acceptance of remaining risks. Here the transition activities are incomplete, so the release should be delayed.

q: A new billing system has passed its tests. The help desk, however, has no release notes, no documented workarounds and no contingency plan. Which kind of readiness is lacking?
options: Data readiness
People readiness
Transition and production support readiness
Cultural readiness
explanation: Transition and production support readiness asks whether operations and support services are ready to answer questions, whether release notes and workarounds are documented, and whether continuity and contingency plans are in place.

q: Staff have been trained on a new system and the servers are ready, but many employees say openly that they will keep using the old spreadsheets, and no one is championing the change. Which kind of readiness is lacking?
options: Cultural readiness
Production environment readiness
Data readiness
People readiness
explanation: Cultural readiness asks whether the organizational culture is supportive of the change, so that people are open-minded, and whether champions are engaged and helping stakeholders see the benefits.

q: A readiness assessment finds that the customer records to be migrated have not been validated. How does Business Analysis for Practitioners say such a gap should be treated?
options: As proof that the project has failed
As a risk to reaching the end state, with a response
As a defect in the acceptance criteria, to be logged
As outside the scope of business analysis
explanation: A readiness assessment identifies gaps in readiness that are considered risks to achieving the end state, along with risk responses for addressing them.

q: At a go/no-go meeting, the decision makers approve releasing the new system to two of five regions now. Is this a "go"?
options: No: a go must release the entire solution
No: a partial release is always a no-go
Only if the sponsor later confirms it in writing
Yes: a go permits release in whole or in part
explanation: A "go" permits the release of the solution in whole or in part. A "no-go" either delays or disapproves the release.
ref: Business Analysis for Practitioners, How to Facilitate Go/No-Go Decision

links.label: Business Analysis for Practitioners, How to Facilitate Go/No-Go Decision

q: An analyst is preparing a go/no-go meeting. The stakeholders have never agreed how the decision will be reached: by vote, by consensus, or by the sponsor alone. What does Business Analysis for Practitioners say about this?
options: It can be settled at the end of the meeting
The analyst should make the decision herself
An agreed decision model should already be in place
The project manager decides during the meeting how they will vote
explanation: An agreed-upon decision model for how to reach a decision should already be in place before the go/no-go decision is made.
ref: Business Analysis for Practitioners, How to Facilitate Go/No-Go Decision

links.label: Business Analysis for Practitioners, How to Facilitate Go/No-Go Decision

q: A company tracks forty measurements of its order process. Management picks three of them as the critical signs of progress toward this year's business objectives. What have these three become?
options: Key performance indicators
Acceptance criteria
Business objectives
Business rules
explanation: Not all metrics are KPIs. A metric becomes a key performance indicator when it is selected as a key indicator of performance critical to achieving specific business objectives. KPIs are not themselves goals or objectives.

q: A project to replace a payroll system lists "convert ten years of employee records" and "train the payroll clerks" among its requirements. Neither will be needed once the new system is running. What kind of requirements are these?
options: Business requirements
Nonfunctional requirements
Transition requirements
Stakeholder requirements
explanation: Transition requirements describe temporary capabilities, such as data conversion, training requirements and operational changes, needed to transition from the current state.
ref: Business Analysis for Practitioners, How to Enable Organizational Transition

links.label: Business Analysis for Practitioners, How to Enable Organizational Transition

q: A bank moves its branches to a new system one region at a time. For some months the old and the new system run side by side. What does Business Analysis for Practitioners call this transition strategy?
options: A massive one-time cutover
A segmented cutover
A readiness assessment
A permanent coexistence
explanation: A segmented cutover moves by segment, for example by region, role or function, and implies temporary coexistence of the replacement with the system being phased out.
ref: Business Analysis for Practitioners, How to Enable Organizational Transition

links.label: Business Analysis for Practitioners, How to Enable Organizational Transition

q: Two years and a large budget have gone into a new system. Tests show serious gaps, yet the steering group says: "We have come too far to stop now. Launch on Monday." What does the practice guide call this?
options: Go fever
Scope creep
Gold plating
Risk appetite
explanation: Go fever comes from the tendency to become overly committed to a chosen course of action because of the time and resources already spent, even when the benefits could be small or the risks significant. A go/no-go decision guards against it.
ref: Business Analysis for Practitioners, Value of Facilitating Go/No-Go Decision

links.label: Business Analysis for Practitioners, Value of Facilitating Go/No-Go Decision

q: Six months after release, a new ordering system is saving far less time than expected. The analyst finds that staff keep a spreadsheet beside it and enter each order twice, because they find one screen awkward. Which typical reason for missed value is this?
options: A technical cause
A regulatory constraint
A missing business case
Workarounds invented by the users
explanation: Typical reasons for missed business value are technical causes, business practices or constraints, resistance to the product or the way it is meant to be used, and opportunistic workarounds devised by users to get around its real or perceived limits.
ref: Business Analysis for Practitioners, How to Evaluate Solution Performance

links.label: Business Analysis for Practitioners, How to Evaluate Solution Performance

q: A new booking service was expected to raise bookings by 10%. After a quarter, they are up by 25%. How does the practice guide say an analyst should treat this variance?
options: As an error in the measurements, to be ignored
As a defect in the service, to be corrected
As an opportunity to analyze and build on
As proof that no further evaluation is needed
explanation: If there is a significant variance between expected and actual value, the analyst analyzes the situation. If the business value exceeds what was expected, it is treated as an opportunity, because the organization can use it to improve the results further.
ref: Business Analysis for Practitioners, How to Evaluate Solution Performance

links.label: Business Analysis for Practitioners, How to Evaluate Solution Performance

q: Acceptance testing found defects. Match each situation with the recommendation.
left: A change in how the business works avoids the defect, with no side effects
The cause is not yet known
People are using the product in a way it was not meant for
explanation: Not every defect needs a change to the product. The analyst may recommend a workaround, a correction of the measurement, an investigation, or an explanation to users; a modification to the product may need a change request.

q: Match each description with the release decision.
left: Part is released and the rest waits
Not yet: something must be finished or fixed first
explanation: The decision is not only yes or no. A partial release puts the ready part into use; a delay waits for something to be finished or fixed.

q: Which release decision is this?

strip.says: Booking and reminders passed acceptance. Payments did not.
Clinics can start using booking and reminders next week.
Payments will follow once the defects are fixed.

options: A partial release
A full release (go)
A delay
A disapproval (no-go)
explanation: In a partial release part of the solution is released and the rest waits. A delay would hold everything back until the payments defects were fixed.
